I'm a bit wary of wholesale importing things from openbmc/pldm.

Added some explanation there of the changes done to the original code.

> I'm a bit wary of wholesale importing things from openbmc/pldm.

I thought that would be the place to find the best pldm related code 😄 with all the best practices.
Hi Alexander, thanks for kicking this off. I do have some reservations, which I've covered inline.

I guess this is in the vein of what libgpiod does with its separate libraries, but I'd like to understand if that's definitely the right direction, rather than providing one library with both C and C++ APIs.

I don't have any preference there.

Probably easier for the user to have a single library.

But since the C++ binding is optional then libpldm != libpldm.

If it's not optional then the size of the library might be too big for some people because of the additional code. Not sure if size is a big topic.

Let me know what you want to go with 👍

Well, we already have the meson option to drop the transport APIs and implementations from the build. I think the specific approach could be more fine-grained, but that depends on people actually caring about it too.

I think it's reasonable to allow customisation. The only trick would be not installing the headers for the symbols that configured out.
Put the functions into 'libpldm' now.
Are the headers installed? Which headers?

They were not installed but the newest revision has an ```install_headers``` statement similar to what is there for libpldm.

Checked with ```DESTDIR=/tmp/install meson install``` that only the headers we want are installed.

I don't like this 😞

The newer libpldm iterator-style APIs are a big improvement. We should do the conversion where necessary.

Implementation of these methods shouldn't be doing any raw indexing into the provided buffer. That's the responsibility of the C APIs.

Makes sense. Agree that the stuff from libpldm should not be re-implemented in the binding.

Since the firmware_update.h header is quite big, can you suggest which functions/macros would be appropriate? I have split the functions here up into more smaller functions, so the indentation should be less and easier to see which does what.

I found several macros (ew, C macros) of the form ```foreach_pldm_*``` in the libpldm headers, but unsure if they are complete (covering all structs) and which is appropriate to use.

Perhaps this is what you meant with
> We should do the conversion where necessary.

? That not all of these iterators are implemented?

> Perhaps this is what you meant with
>
> > We should do the conversion where necessary.
>
> ? That not all of these iterators are implemented?

Yes, not all messages with variable length substructures have iterators. The iterator approach was introduced only recently:

https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/commit/3a2c6589c5660d2066b612bae28ca393a8aa1c2b

> I found several macros (ew, C macros) ... 

I'm not sure how the commentary helps? 

> ... of the form foreach_pldm_* in the libpldm headers

Given the code here, I'd rather than macros.

So to set expectations, currently I don't plan to merge the C++ binding without making improvements to the C API to eliminate most of the implementation of these APIs.

Using the newer iterator macros now, thanks for implementing 😊

Agree the C++ binding should use the most high-level API available from the C side and try to avoid manual memory handling.
Why is this necessary?

It's necessary since the compiler does not accept the implicit conversion in this case. I inlined these expressions and got some errors like below.
```
FAILED: bindings/cxx/libpldmcxx.so.p/package_parser.cpp.o 
c++ -Ibindings/cxx/libpldmcxx.so.p -Ibindings/cxx -I../bindings/cxx -fdiagnostics-color=always -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS=1 -D_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64 -Wall -Winvalid-pch -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -std=c++23 -Og -g -DLIBPLDM_API_DEPRECATED -DLIBPLDM_API_TESTING -fPIC -isystem../include -isysteminclude -MD -MQ bindings/cxx/libpldmcxx.so.p/package_parser.cpp.o -MF bindings/cxx/libpldmcxx.so.p/package_parser.cpp.o.d -o bindings/cxx/libpldmcxx.so.p/package_parser.cpp.o -c ../bindings/cxx/package_parser.cpp
../bindings/cxx/package_parser.cpp: In static member function ‘static std::expected<long unsigned int, std::__cxx11::basic_string<char> > pldm::fw_update::PackageParser::parseCompImageInfoArea(pldm::fw_update::Package&, pldm::fw_update::ComponentImageCount, const std::vector<unsigned char>&, size_t)’:
../bindings/cxx/package_parser.cpp:191:63: error: cannot bind packed field ‘compImageInfo.pldm_component_image_information::comp_identifier’ to ‘short unsigned int&’
  191 |                                                 compImageInfo.comp_identifier,
      |                                                 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
ninja: build stopped: subcommand failed.
```

Ah, well, that's the result of exposing packed structs. Hence:

https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/blob/main/docs/checklists/changes.md?plain=1#L134-L135

Any API making use of packed structs is legacy in my view. This code demonstrates why.
I don't think libraries should be throwing `std::runtime_error()`. You might as well be calling `abort()` in terms of the process life. Libraries can't have that luxury.
removed the exceptions

Why is any of this the responsibility of the binding implementation? All of this should be the responsibility of the C APIs. The C++ APIs should just be a wrapper, improving the ergonomics of the C API using the features of the C++ language.

Having the ```std::format``` strings is nice for debugging in the error case. 
It can provide more information and help to create a correct PLDM package faster.

Instead of having error codes or fixed strings.
So it makes sense to me to have that be part of the binding.

Can we discuss a specific section of code and how it can be better done with an equivalent libpldm call?

'any of this' includes creating the C++ object with the package header information and component info and such, which cannot be done with the C API.

Sorry, my comment wasn't as specific as it should have been. I was not concerned about the use of `std::format`.

The code is parsing the provided message byte buffer. That's not the responsibility of the C++ binding, that's the core responsibility of the (C) library. Internally, libpldm provides a number of mechanisms to ensure spatial memory safety and correct handling of endianness that are both ergonomic to use and generate code with good performance. Specifically, the APIs provided by `src/msgbuf.h`. Those are completely dodged by this implementation. This is not code I wish to maintain. Reviewing stuff like this requires constant vigilance to prevent CVEs (which I will fail at), whereas use of the msgbuf APIs allows me to assume no unsafe accesses are performed or incorrect representations generated, or if there are bugs of this nature, they can be fixed centrally to the benefit of the rest of the library implementation.

There should be C APIs to extract the necessary data to (unpacked) C structs, and from there you can populate your C++ classes (though, possibly it would make sense to embed the C struct as a member in the class). If we do not yet have C APIs to do the job, then it's a deficiency of the (C) library that must first be fixed.
I think the concerns here are fixed with my usage of the newer libpldm iterator macros, otherwise let me know 😊
This is a UUID?

Yes, DSP0267 (version 1.3.0), page 1011, **PackageHeaderIdentifier**
for package format version 1.0
The whitespace thoughout seems quite messed up. I feel like it shouldn't pass clang-format. Does it actually? Are we confident it's actually being processed?

It should be as intended by the .clang-format file.

The indentation is different from what is in the 'pldm' repo, which makes sense since they use different .clang-format files.

```
diff ~/upstreaming/libpldm/.clang-format ~/upstreaming/pldm/.clang-format  | wc -l
221
```

I prefer we design the APIs to conform to `noexcept`. Can you try using `std::expected` instead?

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/expected
Yes, error as value is better 👍. Reworked the functions to return the ```std::expected<T, std::string>```
Is there a reason for this to be virtual? I'd prefer it be static and produce a polymorphic const type rather than mutate an existing instance.

Removed most of the 'virtual' stuff from the newest revision.
Also introduced 'class Package' to represent a PLDM FW Package.

Which can then be separate from the parser.
Going with the comment immediately above, this is why I'm not a fan, because we can instances that are in the zombie state of existing but failed to successfully parse the buffer.

For the new revision, i removed all the instance variables from 'class PackageParser'.

There are now classes 'PackageHeaderInfo' and 'Package' to contain the parsing result.

So the API now primarily has one function to parse the package header, and then the 'parse' function which is static as requested.

It is still 2 function calls to parse, do you want it combined?
Then it would only be one call to parse the entire package.
combined the APIs now to only provide a single call to parse the entire package.
I'd prefer we avoid extension for this. I expect we can handle it directly in the implementation of parse()?
removed the PackageParserV1 class.
This is all a bit much. Can we not use the message structs from the C headers?

Adding `using` aliases for complex generic data structures is one thing, but adding individual `using` aliases for individual message fields is the wrong way to tackle the problem IMO. Pass a pointer/reference to the message struct around instead, and this problem disappears?

Functions defined like below have poor form and are not something I want to maintain:

```
int decode_firmware_device_id_record(
|       const uint8_t *data, size_t length,
|       uint16_t component_bitmap_bit_length,
|       struct pldm_firmware_device_id_record *fw_device_id_record,
|       struct variable_field *applicable_components,
|       struct variable_field *comp_image_set_version_str,
|       struct variable_field *record_descriptors,
|       struct variable_field *fw_device_pkg_data);
```

There are far too many ways to shoot yourself in the foot with this. It's just bad API design. We should try to do better.

Particularly, from [[1](https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/blob/main/docs/checklists/changes.md#philosophy-and-influences)], see:

[How Do I Make This Hard to Misuse?](https://ozlabs.org/~rusty/index.cgi/tech/2008-03-30.html)

and

[What If I Don't Actually Like My Users?](https://ozlabs.org/~rusty/index.cgi/tech/2008-04-01.html)

> That's not really usable, the Component Version String is not in the struct.
So i need to use the using ComponentImageInfo = ....

Right. Both structs you quote use `__attribute__((packed))`, and as outlined in the changes checklist [this is not the desired style moving forward](https://github.com/openbmc/libpldm/blob/main/docs/checklists/changes.md?plain=1#L134-L135). The APIs were created prior to current design tastes and I don't doubt that we could come up with a better design. I'm asking you to do so, in the C APIs, so the C++ APIs remain purely a translation of ergonomics between available language features.

I have reservations about abstracting over the string types. libpldm should not be prescribing any specific string codec implementation. What are your suggestions here? You need to consider the impact of any new dependencies on using libpldm in freestanding applications (host firmware, device firmware, etc). You mustn't assume OpenBMC or glibc.

> I have reservations about abstracting over the string types. libpldm should not be prescribing any specific string codec implementation.

I want to provide an API which is actually useful, and not push all the complexity onto the user. Not aware of any C++ string type which can support all of the string encodings from the spec.

Just passing the plain buffer means every user will have to roll their own code to deal with it or pull in some dependency.

I do not want to use libiconv, utfcpp, or any of the boost stuff and pull it in here.

Changed the implementation of the ```toString``` utility to receive the string type
as argument and return an empty string in case the encoding is unsupported.
Any logic required should exist in the C API and be wrapped by the C++ API. The C++ API should not be providing behaviour beyond the C API.
Removed the ```std::replace_if``` 👍
That's not really resolving my concern, but since it's not part of the public API, then it doesn't matter so much.
Is this header installed?

no, i did not include it in the list in the newest revision.
It's used internally in package_parser.cpp

This should be an array type with choices, like the `oem` option.

```
option('bindings', type: 'array', description: 'Language bindings for libpldm', choices: ['c++'], value: ['c++'])
```
Done. A little surprised that you consider the binding as enabled by default.

All options need to be enabled by default so that they are exercised by CI.

I believe it depends on the package routing. If you go via bmcweb/redfish then the update is performed via dbus and the dbus fw inventory. In the new design 
https://github.com/openbmc/docs/blob/master/designs/code-update.md
the package has PLDM format. So if the component is not managed by the specific code updater, it may not even receive the update package.

> Bitmap of which firmware components are applicable to FDs which match this Device Identifier
record. A set bit N indicates the Nth (0-based) component in the payload (which is described by the Nth entry in the component information area of the package header) is applicable to this device.

The whole point is to associate component images with a firmware device.

I'm proposing we stash the bitmap as-is for now, until we've processed all the component images. After that can create a structure that directly lists the component images for a given firmware device, rather than leaving it to the library consumer to resolve the images from the bitmap themselves. That way we're not exposing this variable-length bitmap with slightly troubling semantics (regarding the potential discrepancy between the available bits and the number of component images), or just a raw list of indexes. > If we access these new struct members, then the application will no longer link against older libpldm versions, right? Which is the same failure mode as my patch.

No. I feel you haven't absorbed the design of the new package parsing APIs and the impact of the package pin, which is an approach based on existing practices to solve this problem: [LWN - Conventions for extensible system calls](https://lwn.net/Articles/830666/).

The constraint is that the relevant structures must _only_ grow, they must never have their members reordered or removed.

There are several things at play here:

1. API: The source-level types and function prototypes that we program applications against
2. ABI: The target-specific assumptions derived from the source definitions, and encoded in the consuming application binary and the library shared object

Particularly, for the ABI, the properties (sizes and offsets) of types are separately encoded in both the application binary and the library shared object. There are no linked symbols for struct members, just offsets encoded in the instruction stream. These offsets are derived from the API - the source headers for the library.

We're considering an application binary:

1. Compiled against version `N` of libpldm (API)
2. Dynamically linked against libpldm version `N-1` (ABI)

For the purpose of the discussion, the only API change between `N-1` and `N` is the implementation of a (hypothetical) new firmware update package format revision from DSP0267, where additional members have been defined in one or more of of the firmware device, downstream device, or component image info records.

The new C API struct sizes understood by the application will be larger than those understood by the library, but that's it. The APIs are designed such that the application allocates the relevant objects (usually on the stack) and passes a pointer into the library APIs, and the library fills them out or otherwise consumes them. As the size of the object referenced by the pointer provided by the application will always be sized at least as large as the library's expectations, and the layout to that point must match, all accesses are safe despite the difference in understanding of the ABI between the application and the library. Put another way, the new C package parsing APIs don't allocate and can't therefore return a pointer to an object of an unexpected size with respect to the application. This would be risky behaviour, and is why the API is designed to not do so.

By design (and construction of the scenario), the set of function symbols exported by the library do not change.

From here it comes down to how the application specifies the package pin:

1. The application, compiled against version `N`, specifies the pin for highest format revision supported in version `N` of libpldm
2. The application, compiled against version `N`, specifies the pin for highest format revision supported in version `N-1` of libpldm

Bearing in mind the application binary compiled against version `N` of libpldm is dynamically linking against version `N-1`, both cases link successfully, as no new function symbols are introduced. However, case 1 results in an error returned from `decode_pldm_firmware_update_package()` due to the unrecognised package pin provided by the application. Case 2 suffers no failures - despite the application being aware of the increased size of the relevant structs, neither the application nor libpldm will be accessing those members by assertion of the pin, and so the decoding process continues.

By contrast, the D-Pointer approach with explicit accessor methods for the C++ binding yields a link failure for case 1, but likely not for case 2 (as the new symbols won't be referenced).
